Florida Wildlife Weekly

Week of Aug 31 – Sep 6, 2026

Nesting records, manatee protection, Everglades fire & drought, and a sneaky new invasive.

Every Sunday morning, I put together a weekly roundup of everything that happened in Florida wildlife the week before — sightings, rescues, research, the weird stuff, the wonderful stuff. Florida’s got more wild going on than almost anywhere, and this is your one-stop look at it. Grab your coffee, settle in, and let’s see what the state’s critters are up to!

Steve Barlow
Certified Wildlife Biologist

🐢 Space Coast turtles are rewriting the record books
Loggerhead sea turtle · Wikimedia Commons

Canaveral National Seashore has already logged more than 17,000 sea turtle nests this year, past its previous high of 16,000-plus from 2023. Down the coast, Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge has broken a loggerhead record that stood since 1998 — more than 21,800 loggerhead nests so far, with nesting still running through October.

Boca Raton is having a moment too: the city’s Gumbo Limbo nest page now lists 1,118 loggerheads (a city record), plus record leatherbacks (43) and 150 greens.

Great news for Florida’s beaches. Just remember: hatchlings still have boats, lights, and plastics waiting for them once they leave the sand.

FOX 35 Orlando · Boca nest tracker

🏖️ Beach weekend etiquette, from FWC
Florida sea turtle (illustrative) · Wikimedia Commons

With Labor Day behind us and hatchlings still emerging, FWC reminded beachgoers that nesting isn’t over. Flightless shorebird chicks may still be around, and migrating piping plovers and red knots are heading back.

The short version: stay 50+ feet away, keep lights off and curtains closed after dark, fill holes and pack up gear, leash dogs, skip beach fireworks, and call 888-404-FWCC if you find a turtle in trouble.

FWC Labor Day beach tips

🐋 Clearwater moves to slow boats for Stevenson Creek manatees
Florida manatee · Wikimedia Commons

Clearwater City Council unanimously advanced a year-round minimum-wake / manatee protection zone for Stevenson Creek, a shallow ~3.2-mile tidal estuary. Better water quality has been drawing manatees and calves; citizen science linked to Save the Manatee Club counted 200+ animals over eight months, and FWC data notes at least three watercraft deaths in or near the creek.

Important caveat: the ordinance still needs FWC approval, permits, and markers before it’s live.

Tampa Bay Beacons · Bay News 9

🔥 Everglades: fire, drought, and Shark Valley back open
Everglades sawgrass prairie · Wikimedia Commons

NPS reopened the Shark Valley District on August 24 after wildfire closures. As of reopen: Chipmunk Fire ~17,000 acres / 60% contained; Movie Dome and Vulture fires fully contained. WLRN reported extreme drought across the central Everglades, low water conservation areas, high Florida Bay salinity concerns, and peat-burn risk — with scientists warning recovery could take years.

Visitor win (Shark Valley’s open again). Habitat story still heavy.

NPS · WLRN

🐍 Asian swamp eels show up in Loxahatchee
Asian swamp eel · Wikimedia Commons

Researchers confirmed invasive Asian swamp eels in Arthur R. Marshall Loxahatchee National Wildlife Refuge. They eat crayfish, frogs, and small fish that wading birds depend on, can breathe air and ride out drought, and are tough to detect or trap.

Some scientists warn food-web impacts could rival — or in some wetland contexts exceed — pythons. That’s expert caution, not settled consensus, but it’s a story worth watching.

Palm Beach Post

🐦 Florida Bay’s wading-bird season, by the numbers
Great egret hunting in Florida Bay · Wikimedia Commons

Audubon Florida’s Everglades Research Station wrapped summer monitoring: nesting at 55 of 75 surveyed sites, 1,819 nests among priority Egretta species (Tricolored Heron leading at 1,269), and about 3,000 nests across the broader season. Eighteen species nested overall.

Wading birds are one of the best pulse-checks we have on Everglades health — especially in a drought year.

Audubon Florida

🐻 Mark your calendar: bear harvest permits open Sept. 11
Florida black bear · Wikimedia Commons

FWC says applications for the 2026 regulated bear harvest open 10 a.m. EDT September 11 through September 21. Drawing is random; $5 to apply; permits $100 resident / $300 nonresident. Season runs December 5–27 in four zones. Apply at GoOutdoorsFlorida.com.

FWC

🐊 Alligator hatchling season is still peaking
American alligator · Wikimedia Commons

Mid-August through early September means new gators — and more protective moms. Swim only in designated areas in daylight, never feed alligators, keep pets leashed away from water, call 866-FWC-GATOR for nuisance animals (911 for emergencies).

MySuncoast / FWC tips
